check:0:0.q: Why not “The test set was too small”?
check:0:0.a:
"The test set was too small" has a grain of truth. A smaller test set does make it easier for a rare group to get left out by luck. With 15 refund-fraud questions out of 300, a random split might put three in test, or two, or none.

But size isn't the root cause. A bigger test set only lowers the odds of missing the group. It never guarantees the group shows up. It also takes examples away from dev, where you do your tuning. And the same problem can hit dev or holdout too.

The real issue is that a plain random split ignores groups. It treats all 300 examples as one pile. Rare groups are then at the mercy of chance.

**Stratifying** fixes that. It means splitting each group on its own. You deal the 15 fraud questions across dev, test and holdout, then do the same for every other group. Now every set gets fraud questions, whatever its size.

"The split wasn't stratified, so a small group could miss a set entirely" is better because it names the actual cause and points straight to the fix.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Refund fraud questions are too hard to evaluate”?
check:0:1.a:
That option sounds plausible, because refund-fraud questions may well be tricky. But difficulty isn't the problem described here. The problem is that the test set has *zero* of them. A hard question can still be evaluated. You just need some of them in the set to measure how the app does.

What went wrong is the split itself. 15 out of 300 is a small group. A plain random split gives no guarantee that each group lands in every set. So a small group can end up missing from one set entirely, and that is what happened here.

"Too hard to evaluate" also points you toward the wrong fix: dropping or ignoring those questions. That hides a weak spot instead of measuring it.

The real fix is to **stratify**, which means treating refund fraud as its own group. You then deal its examples across dev, test and holdout, like dealing cards from a separate deck.

The better answer names the actual cause: an unstratified random split can leave a small group out of a set entirely, and stratifying prevents that.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Nothing, more checks find more bugs”?
check:1:0.a:
That answer gets one thing right. Checking your work often really does catch problems early. That habit is good. It just belongs on the dev set.

What it misses is the test set's job. The test set is meant to tell you how your app will do on questions it has never been tuned for. That only works if your changes were never shaped by it.

Each time you check the test set and then tweak the prompt, you nudge the prompt toward those exact examples. Do that all week and the prompt slowly fits those specific questions. This is called **overfitting**: doing well on the examples you studied, but not on new ones.

So the test score climbs, but it no longer predicts how real users will fare. You haven't found more bugs. You've lost your honest measuring stick.

The fix is simple. Iterate on dev as much as you like, and touch test only before a release.

"You're tuning against the test set" is better because it names the real problem: repeated looking-and-changing turns the test set into a second dev set, so its score stops being trustworthy.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The test set is too small to use”?
check:1:2.a:
"The test set is too small to use" points at a real worry, but not the one in this question.

**What it gets right:** a small test set can give a shaky score. With only a few examples, one lucky or unlucky answer moves the number a lot. That is worth thinking about when you build your sets.

**What it misses:** the question says nothing about size. The problem is the habit of checking the test set after every change. Each time you look and then tweak your prompt, you nudge it toward doing well on *those exact examples*. After a week, the score mostly tells you how well you fit the test set. It no longer tells you how the app will do on new questions.

A bigger test set would not fix this. Tuning against it would spoil it just the same, only more slowly. That is why the lesson gives each set one job: tweak freely against the dev set, and check the test set rarely, just before a release.

"You're tuning against the test set" is better because it names the real mistake: using the test set like a dev set makes its score dishonest, whatever its size.

judge.notes: Minor: the claims about small sets giving shaky scores and about a bigger set spoiling 'more slowly' go beyond the lesson, though they don't contradict it, and the length is right at the 200-word limit.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Write another 100 questions by hand”?
check:2:0.a:
Writing another 100 questions by hand does get one thing right. More checked examples make your eval set bigger and steadier, and hand-checked questions are reliable. That is why the lesson keeps a **golden** set: a fixed group of examples you checked yourself.

But the new questions come from the same place as the old ones: your own head. You would write them in your own style, about the topics you expect. Real users don't work that way. They make typos. They ask vague or odd questions. They bring up things that changed since last year. A bigger pile of your own guesses is still a guess about how the app is used.

It also skips the bugs you already know about. Mistakes the app made before won't show up unless you deliberately add them back.

"Add real traffic and past failures" is the better answer. A sample of recent real questions shows how people actually use the app today, and past failures make sure old mistakes stay fixed.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Ask a model to make up more questions”?
check:2:1.a:
Asking a model to make up more questions does get one thing right: it gives you more examples, quickly and cheaply. That can help fill a thin group, like refund questions, when you have very few.

But the Check question asks what would make the set **closer to how the app is really used**. Made-up questions can't do that. A model writes what it *imagines* users ask. Real users type short, messy questions with typos, mix two topics, or ask about things that changed since last year. A model tends to write clean, tidy questions in its own style. Those are often easier for another model to answer, so your scores can look better than reality.

Made-up questions also miss your **past failures**, the exact cases where the app went wrong before. A model has no idea which ones those were.

So you'd have a bigger set, but not a more realistic one.

"Add real traffic and past failures" is better because it brings in questions real users actually asked, plus the mistakes you never want to repeat, so the eval set reflects real use.

judge.notes: No real problems; the points about messy real queries and model-written questions being too tidy go beyond the lesson but do not contradict it.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “A counter per group” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer**

**The problem.** "A plain random split can leave a small group, like refunds, out of the test set completely. Then the test score tells you nothing about refunds."

**The idea.** "So I deal each group separately, like cards from its own deck. I keep a counter for every group. Each example looks up its group's count and takes that slot in a fixed pattern: three dev, one test, one holdout. Then the pattern starts again. Every set ends up with every group in about the same proportions, and it only walks through the list once."

**The trade-off.** "The pattern is fixed, so the list must be shuffled first. Otherwise the original order of the data decides the split. Also, a group with fewer than five examples can't reach every set."

**A likely follow-up**

*"What if several questions come from the same user?"*

Hint for a strong answer: bring up the leakage rule. Leakage means a set gets clues it shouldn't have. Say you'd deal whole users, or whole documents, instead of single questions, so related examples stay in one set. Admit the proportions then become only roughly equal.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
Here are the signs that the split was skipped or done wrong.

**A group is missing or tiny in test.** You look at per-group scores and `refunds` is blank, or rests on one example. That usually means a plain random split, not a stratified one. Stratified means each group is dealt across the sets in the same proportions.

**Scores move when the app didn't change.** If test is mostly `billing` while dev is heavy on `refunds`, the overall score shifts because the mix differs, not because your prompt got better or worse.

**A great eval score that drops in real use.** Common causes:
- Leakage: the same user or document shows up in more than one set.
- A holdout that was looked at and tuned against, so it is no longer honest.
- No recent real traffic in the set.

**Old bugs come back.** Past failures were never added to the set.

**Results nobody can compare.** Nobody knows which set version, like `faq-v4`, was used.

**Quickest check:** count examples per group in each set and compare the proportions. Then confirm no user ID or document ID appears in more than one set.

learn:stops.a:
The dealing method works well in the common case. Here are three places it needs extra care.

**Very small groups.** If a group has only two or three examples, a 3-dev, 1-test, 1-holdout pattern leaves test or holdout without that group. Collect or write more examples for rare groups, or merge tiny groups into a broader one. Then check that every set really contains every group.

**Data that changes over time.** Real user questions drift. Drift means new products, new wording and new problems appear. A set built from last year's traffic can look great while today's users struggle. Add fresh traffic regularly, and save each refresh under a new version name like `faq-v5` so old and new scores aren't mixed up.

**Bundles that must stay together.** Sometimes one user or one document has many questions, spread across several groups. Dealing single examples would split that bundle across sets, which is leakage. Leakage means the app has effectively seen test material during tuning. Instead, deal whole bundles, keeping each user's or document's questions in one set. Group proportions then come out roughly even rather than exact.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the answer stays within the lesson, gives three concrete cases with fixes, is about 180 words, and does not give the solution.

learn:term.q: How is “golden” different from “recent real traffic”?
learn:term.a:
Both feed your eval set, but they do different jobs.

The **golden** set is fixed. You chose each question and checked its correct answer by hand. It only changes when you decide, and each version gets a name like `faq-v4`. Its job is **stability**: the same questions every run, so you can fairly compare today's prompt with last week's.

**Recent real traffic** is a sample of questions real users asked lately. Nobody wrote them for testing. Its job is **realism**: it shows what people actually ask now, with messy wording and topics you never thought of.

Think of a driving test. The golden set is the fixed exam route, the same turns every time, so scores compare fairly. Real traffic is a drive through town today. It is less controlled but closer to real life.

They work together. Golden keeps results comparable. Traffic keeps them honest. Say users suddenly ask lots of `refunds` questions your golden set barely covers. Traffic exposes that gap, and you might add some to the next version. Then you deal both across dev, test and holdout by group: `billing`, `shipping`, `refunds`.

judge.notes: No real problems. The 'stability' and 'realism' labels and the refunds scenario go slightly beyond the lesson's wording, but they fit it and do not contradict it.

check:0:0.q: Why not “The model is excellent: 0.97 means near perfect”?
check:0:0.a:
**Why "0.97 means near perfect" isn't the best answer**

It gets one thing right. A ROC-AUC of 0.97 is real. It means a random fraud usually gets a higher score than a random normal transaction. The model has learned something.

What it misses is how rare fraud is. With 1 fraud in 200, there are 199 normal transactions for every fraud. Most of them are easy to rank below the fraud. ROC-AUC counts all those easy wins, so the score looks great. That's what "flatters" means here: it makes the model look better than it is for this job.

PR-AUC (average precision) tells a different story. Walk down the list from the highest score. Each time you reach a real fraud, note the precision so far. Precision is the share of flagged items that are really fraud. Those precisions average about 0.18. So at those points, only about 18% of the flagged transactions are fraud. The rest are false alarms. That beats the random baseline of 0.005 (1 in 200), but it's far from "near perfect."

**Why the other option is better:** "ROC-AUC flatters it; PR-AUC says most alerts are false alarms" is right because it reads both numbers honestly for a rare event.

judge.notes: No major problem. The answer is about 200 words, slightly long, and the 'about 18% of flagged are fraud' line loosely equates average precision with precision at a single point.

check:0:2.q: Why not “PR-AUC must be a bug when ROC-AUC is this high”?
check:0:2.a:
It's a fair instinct to double-check when two metrics disagree. Checking that labels and scores weren't swapped is a good habit. But here the gap isn't a bug. It's exactly what rare positives do.

Picture 10,000 transactions: 50 fraud, 9,950 legit. ROC-AUC 0.97 means a random fraud case usually scores above a random legit one. That sounds great. But even if only 3% of legit transactions score high, that's about 300 false alarms crowding the top of the list. The 50 real frauds are mixed in among them. So when you walk down the list, precision (the share of flagged items that are really fraud) stays low. That's why PR-AUC is 0.18.

ROC-AUC looks good because thousands of easy legit transactions are ranked correctly. Those easy wins hide the crowded top.

Also remember PR-AUC's baseline. Random guessing scores the share of positives, which is 1 in 200, or 0.005. So 0.18 is far better than random. It's just honest about the false alarms.

"ROC-AUC flatters it; PR-AUC says most alerts are false alarms" is better because it explains the gap as the expected effect of rare positives, not a mistake.

check:1:0.a:
"It's close to perfect" gets the direction backwards. For PR-AUC, bigger is better, and a perfect model scores 1.0. A score of 0.01 is about as far from 1.0 as you can get.

The mix-up is understandable. Some numbers, like an error rate or a loss (a number that measures how wrong the model is), are best when they are near 0. PR-AUC is not one of those. It measures how well the real positives (here, orders that really got returned) land near the top of the ranked list.

What that answer misses is the baseline. The baseline is what random guessing would score. For PR-AUC, the baseline is the share of positives, not 0.5. Here 1 in 100 orders is returned, so the share is 0.01. A model that just shuffled the orders randomly would score about 0.01 too.

So this model ranks returns no better than a coin-flip-style shuffle.

**"It's about as good as guessing" is the right answer, because 0.01 matches the 1% share of returns, which is exactly what random guessing scores.**

check:1:1.q: Why not “It must be a bug”?
check:1:1.a:
"It must be a bug" comes from a fair instinct. A score of 0.01 looks shockingly low. If you're used to ROC-AUC, where guessing scores 0.5, then 0.01 seems impossible without a mistake. A quick sanity check of your code is never a bad habit.

But that answer misses what the number is telling you. PR-AUC's baseline (what random guessing scores) is the share of positives. Here, 1 in 100 orders gets returned, so the share is 0.01. A model that ranks orders at random would score about 0.01.

So nothing is broken. The math is working fine. The result is just bad news about the model. It isn't putting the real returns near the top of the list any better than chance would. Blaming a bug could send you hunting for an error that isn't there, when the real job is to improve the model.

"It's about as good as guessing" is better because it matches 0.01 against the right baseline, the 1% share of returns, and reads the score correctly.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Accuracy, to back up the 0.95”?
check:2:0.a:
Asking for a second number is a good instinct. The 0.95 does need backing up. Accuracy just backs it up with the wrong kind of number.

**Accuracy** is the share of all predictions that were correct. With rare events, that share is mostly made of easy negatives. Say 1 machine in 100 fails. A model that always says "no failure" is right 99 times out of 100. That is 99% accuracy, yet it catches zero failures. So accuracy flatters the model in the same way ROC-AUC does. Both get inflated by all those easy negatives.

Accuracy also depends on one threshold. That is the score cutoff where you switch from "no failure" to "failure." So it judges a single setting, not the model across every threshold. Neither number would tell you whether the real failures actually show up near the top of the list.

**"PR-AUC for the same model"** is the better ask. It rewards ranking the real failures near the top. Its baseline is the share of positives, about 0.01 here, not 0.5. That makes it the honest score for rare events like machine failures.

judge.notes: No blocking problems. Minor: the PR-AUC part runs four sentences instead of the requested one, and 'baseline' is not explained as 'what random guessing scores'.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Nothing: 0.95 is close to perfect”?
check:2:2.a:
The answer gets one thing right. A ROC-AUC of 0.95 is real information. It means a random failure gets a higher score than a random normal machine 95% of the time. That is far better than guessing, which scores 0.5.

What it misses is that failures are rare. When almost every example is a negative (really 0), there are huge numbers of easy normal machines to rank below the failures. That pads ROC-AUC and flatters the model.

Picture 10,000 normal machines and 10 failures. Being "95% right" still leaves about 5% of the normals, roughly 500, scoring above a typical failure. So a technician checking the top of the list could face around 50 false alarms for every real failure. ROC-AUC alone hides that.

PR-AUC exposes it. It rewards real positives (examples that are really 1) found near the top of the list. Its baseline is the share of positives, here about 0.001, not 0.5.

So "PR-AUC for the same model" is the better answer, because it shows whether the alerts at the top of the list are actually worth acting on when failures are rare.

judge.notes: The 500 and 50 false-alarm figures go beyond the lesson, but they are consistent with a 0.95 ROC-AUC on 10,000 normals and 10 failures. The answer is about 187 words, so it stays under the limit.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Sort by score, then walk down” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* Precision and recall change with the threshold. That's the cut-off score where we say "yes, this is a 1." I want one number that judges the model across every threshold.

*The idea:* Sort the examples by score, highest first, like ranking exam papers. Walk down the list. Each time I reach a real positive, I note the precision so far: the share of examples passed that were really positive. Average those notes. That's average precision, the usual way to compute PR-AUC. It rewards putting the real positives near the top.

*A trade-off:* It only looks at the order of the scores, not their size. A model can rank well and still give scores that don't match real probabilities.

**A likely follow-up:** "Why not just use ROC-AUC?"

*Hint for a strong answer:* When positives are rare, there are many easy negatives to rank below them. That makes ROC-AUC look flattering. Then mention the baseline. Random guessing on PR-AUC scores about the share of positives, around 0.01 for 1% positives, not 0.5. So you compare a PR-AUC score against that baseline, not against 0.5.

judge.notes: No real problems. The 'order not size of scores' trade-off is not in the lesson, but it is true and does not contradict it. The answer is about 188 words, just under the limit.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **ROC-AUC looks great, real use disappoints.** You report a ROC-AUC (the "chance a real positive outranks a negative" score) of 0.95. Then in production, the top of your alert list is mostly false alarms. That's ROC-AUC flattering you, because rare positives sit above a crowd of easy negatives.
- **PR-AUC judged against the wrong baseline.** A PR-AUC (area under the precision-recall curve) of 0.15 can sound poor. With 1% positives it's 15 times better than guessing. And 0.5 doesn't mean "random" here.
- **Only ROC-AUC in your logs.** If your MLflow run (one logged experiment) has `roc_auc` but no `pr_auc`, the honest number for rare events was never looked at.
- **Your hand-made score disagrees with the library.** This often means the list was sorted lowest-first by mistake.

**Quickest check**

1. Work out the share of positives in your data. Compare PR-AUC to it, not to 0.5.
2. Sort by score and read the top 20 examples. Count how many are really positive. If few are, the high ROC-AUC was misleading.
3. Compare your number with `average_precision_score` on the same data.

learn:stops.a:
Average precision is a strong default for rare events, but here are three places it needs extra care.

**1. The share of positives changes over time.** Random guessing scores about the share of positives, so the "floor" moves when that share moves. A PR-AUC of 0.30 means more when positives are 1% of the data than when they are 20%. Always log the share of positives next to `pr_auc`, and compare a score against that baseline.

**2. Very few real positives.** With only a handful of real 1s, one example moving up or down the list can swing the score a lot. Gather more labeled positives if you can. Otherwise, check how much the score shifts when you re-run on different random samples, and treat small differences as noise.

**3. Retrieval in a RAG app.** RAG means "retrieval-augmented generation": the app fetches documents, then an LLM answers from them. Usually only the top few fetched documents reach the LLM, so a good ranking far down the list doesn't help. Measure precision or recall within the top few results instead.

learn:term.a:
They're two views of the same idea. One is the goal and the other is the recipe.

**PR-AUC** is the goal. Picture a curve of precision against recall, one point per threshold. PR-AUC is the area under that curve. Precision means "of what I flagged, how much was real?" Recall means "of all the real ones, how much did I find?"

**Average precision** is the recipe. You walk down the list once, from highest score to lowest. At each real positive, you note the precision so far. Then you average those notes. In the lesson's example, that gives (1.00 + 0.67 + 0.60) / 3, about 0.76.

**How they fit together:** average precision is a step-by-step way to measure that area without drawing anything. Each real positive adds one step to recall. The precision at that moment is the height of that step. That's why libraries like scikit-learn report PR-AUC with `average_precision_score`.

**Everyday comparison:** PR-AUC is "the area of this room." Average precision is counting the floor tiles to get it. Another method, like drawing slanted lines between points, can give a slightly different number. So say which method you used.

judge.notes: The answer passes every check. It is about 190 words. The remark about slanted lines giving a slightly different number goes beyond the lesson, but it is true and does not contradict it.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Nothing: the threshold stays at 90, where it wa…”?
check:0:0.a:
"Nothing" gets one thing right. The number in the rule really is still 90. Nobody changed the setting.

What it misses is what that number *means*. The rule assumes "92% sure" means "right about 92% of the time." The reliability table shows that isn't true here. In the 80-100% bucket the model's average prediction was 0.92, but only 61% of those predictions turned out right.

The scores above 90% sit inside that bucket. The table doesn't show their exact hit rate on their own. Still, the bucket they belong to was right far less often than the model claimed. So you have no reason to trust a 90%+ score to mean what it says.

That is the point of calibration. A threshold is only as good as the probabilities feeding it. The rule looks safe on paper. In practice it may wave through many more mistakes than anyone expected, with no person checking them.

"Overconfident: the rule approves far more mistakes than it seems" is better because it names the real problem. The model's high scores overstate how often it's right, so the 90% bar doesn't give the safety it promises.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the closing explanation runs to two sentences rather than the requested one, which is minor.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Underconfident: the threshold could safely be l…”?
check:0:2.a:
"Underconfident" gets one thing right: the 80-100% bucket is badly off. The model's 0.92 and the real 0.61 are far apart, so something is wrong there.

But it points the wrong way. **Underconfident** means the model says a lower probability than it should. An underconfident model would say 60% when the thing really happens 90% of the time. Here it's the reverse. The model says 92%, but only 61% of those cases really happened. Its confidence is *higher* than reality. That is **overconfidence**.

That also flips the advice. Lowering the threshold would let even more predictions through the auto-approve gate. Many of those would be wrong. The problem gets worse, not better.

Think about what "auto-approve above 90%" seems to promise. It sounds like "we only approve when we're 90%+ sure." In this bucket, though, roughly 4 in 10 of those approvals are mistakes. The threshold looks safe, but it isn't.

"Overconfident: the rule approves far more mistakes than it seems" is better because it reads the gap in the right direction. It also names the real cost: hidden errors slipping past an approval rule that looks safe.

judge.notes: Minor: it treats the 80-100% bucket as if it were the 'above 90%' rule, and says 'many of those would be wrong' about a lowered threshold without lesson support, but both are reasonable inferences.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Trust it: the model knows itself”?
check:1:1.a:
It's tempting, but "Trust it: the model knows itself" skips the one step that matters.

**What it gets right:** a confidence number *can* drive a decision. The lesson's own example is "auto-approve above 90%, send to a person below." So wanting to use that 95% isn't wrong.

**What it misses:** the 95% is the model's claim, not proof. The lesson warns that LLMs asked to rate their own confidence are often **overconfident**. That means they say a higher number than their real hit rate. Look at the lesson's table. In the 80-100% bucket, the model's average prediction was 0.92, but the thing really happened only 0.61 of the time. If you auto-approved those, you'd let through far more mistakes than you planned.

An overconfident model makes your threshold mean something it does not. "Above 90%" would sound safe while being much riskier.

**Why "Check how often its 95% answers are right" is better:** it tests whether the model is **calibrated** (its stated confidence matches how often it's actually right) before you let that number make decisions for you.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Raise the threshold to 99% and release it”?
check:1:2.a:
"Raise the threshold to 99% and release it" has one good instinct. It tries to be more careful before letting answers through without a person looking at them.

But it skips the real question. A threshold is a cut-off line, like "auto-approve above 90%." That line only works if the model's numbers are honest. The lesson calls this **calibration**: when a model says 95%, it should be right about 95% of the time.

You don't know yet whether this LLM's 95% is honest. The lesson warns that LLMs rating their own confidence are often overconfident. Moving the line to 99% doesn't test that. You'd still be trusting the model's own numbers without checking them. If those numbers are off, a higher line doesn't fix them.

So the problem isn't where the line sits. It's that nobody has checked what the numbers mean.

"Check how often its 95% answers are right" is better because it measures whether the model's confidence matches what really happens before you build a decision on it.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Model B, it plays it safe”?
check:2:1.a:
"Plays it safe" sounds sensible. A cautious model can feel safer than a bold one. But the Brier score doesn't tell you Model B is cautious. It only tells you how far its chances land from what really happened.

Quick reminder: the Brier score takes the gap between each predicted chance and the real result (1 if the customer cancelled, 0 if not), multiplies the gap by itself, and averages. Lower is better.

Model B's score matches the score of always guessing 50%. So, on average, its chances are no closer to the truth than a model that knows nothing about the customers. Whatever it is doing, it isn't adding useful information. Calling that "safe" gives it credit the score doesn't support.

This matters when the chance drives a decision, like "contact the customer if cancel risk is above 70%." If Model B's chances are no better than the know-nothing baseline, that threshold can't be trusted.

Model A is the better answer because a Brier score close to 0 means its chances sit close to what really happened, so you can act on them.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Neither: Brier can't compare them”?
check:2:2.a:
It's a fair instinct to be cautious about one number. A single score can hide details. A Brier score won't tell you *which* buckets are off, the way a reliability diagram (the chart comparing predicted chances with what really happened) does.

But comparing models is exactly what the Brier score is for. Both models predict the same thing: whether each customer cancels. So their scores sit on the same scale, and lower means better.

Here's what each score says:

- **Model B** scores about 0.25. That's what you get by always saying "50%". Its chances tell you no more than a coin flip.
- **Model A** scores close to 0. For each customer, it gives a high chance to those who cancel and a low chance to those who stay. Its gaps between prediction and outcome are tiny.

A Brier score near 0 is hard to reach with dishonest probabilities. An overconfident model would get punished. Every "92%" that turns out wrong adds a big squared gap (the gap multiplied by itself).

**Model A is the better answer because its Brier score near 0 means its predicted chances closely match what really happened, while Model B's matches a coin flip.**

judge.notes: Minor: it runs slightly over 200 words, and 'hard to reach with dishonest probabilities' goes a little beyond the lesson, but nothing contradicts it.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Five buckets with running totals” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**The 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "I want to know if a model's probabilities are honest. When it says 90%, is it right about 90% of the time?"

*The idea:* "I sort each prediction into one of five buckets by its probability, like sorting mail into slots. For each bucket I keep running totals: how many predictions landed there, the sum of their probabilities, and how many really happened. That takes one walk through the data. Then I put each bucket's average prediction next to how often the thing really happened. If the two match, the model is calibrated, meaning its confidence is honest."

*The trade-off:* "Five buckets is a choice. More buckets show more detail, but each one holds fewer predictions, so its numbers get noisy. An empty bucket gets skipped, so I never divide by zero."

**A likely follow-up**

"Why not just report accuracy?"

*Hint at a strong answer:* Accuracy only counts right versus wrong. It ignores how confident the model was. Then tie it to a decision. If you auto-approve above 90%, you need "90%" to really mean 90%. You can also mention the Brier score, which sums up calibration and accuracy in one number.

judge.notes: No real problems. The Brier line ('sums up calibration and accuracy') goes slightly beyond the lesson's wording but is not wrong, and the length is right at the limit.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The top bucket lies.** In the 80-100% bucket, the average prediction is far above how often it really happened. The lesson's table shows this: 0.92 predicted, 0.61 real.
- **Auto-approve lets mistakes through.** Items above your 90% threshold go straight through, yet people later find many of them wrong. The threshold no longer means "safe".
- **Everything looks confident.** Most predictions sit at 90% or higher. LLMs rating their own confidence often do this.
- **Good accuracy, bad probabilities.** Accuracy (how often the model is right overall) can look fine while the probabilities are still off. If you never logged a Brier score, nobody checked.
- **A Brier score near 0.25.** That is what always guessing 50% scores. Your model is barely beating a coin.

**Quickest check**

Take a recent batch of predictions where you now know what really happened. Sort them into bins by probability. In each bin, compare the average prediction with the share that really happened. Look hardest at the top bin, because that is where your decisions get made.

Also check how many predictions each bin holds. A bin with only a handful can look wrong just by chance.

learn:stops.a:
Calibration checks work best with plenty of steady data. Here are three places they need extra care.

**Very little data.** With only a few predictions in a bucket, the "really happened" share jumps around by luck. Use fewer buckets, and treat the table as a rough hint until you have hundreds of predictions.

**Data that changes over time.** A model that was calibrated last spring can drift once users or topics change. Recheck on recent predictions regularly, and record the Brier score each time in MLflow (a tool that keeps a log of results from each run) so you can spot it creeping up.

**LLMs rating their own confidence.** A chatbot saying "I'm 90% sure" is not a measured probability, and these self-ratings often bunch near the top. Test them on a labelled set (examples where you already know the right answer), and if they are off, adjust or replace them before trusting any auto-approve threshold.

judge.notes: Minor: 'bunch near the top' goes slightly beyond the lesson, which only says LLM self-ratings are often overconfident, but it is consistent with that and not wrong.

learn:term.a:
**Calibration** means a model's probabilities can be taken at face value. When it says "70% likely," the thing should really happen about 70% of the time.

Think of a weather forecaster. Look at all the days they said "70% chance of rain." If it rained on about 7 out of every 10 of those days, the forecaster is calibrated. If it rained on only 4 of them, their "70%" was too confident.

The lesson checks a model the same way. It sorts predictions into buckets by probability. Then it compares two numbers in each bucket: the average prediction, and how often the thing really happened.

In the example table:

- **0-20% bucket:** average prediction 0.12, really happened 0.10. Close, so calibrated there.
- **40-60% bucket:** 0.51 versus 0.48. Also close.
- **80-100% bucket:** 0.92 versus 0.61. Far apart. The model sounded about 92% sure but was right only 61% of the time. That is **overconfidence**.

This matters when a decision rests on the number. A threshold like "auto-approve above 90%" assumes the model's high scores are trustworthy. This table shows its high-confidence bucket is not.

check:0:0.q: Why not “The new version is clearly better, so ship it”?
check:0:0.a:
"Ship it" gets one thing right. The count does favour the new version. Three more questions passed, and counting the disagreements is how you decide a comparison.

What it misses is the reading. You changed the **reranker**, the step that reorders retrieved documents so the best ones come first. So the improvements should trace back to documents. You would expect causes like "moved the right doc up."

Instead, every improvement says "answer is shorter." A reranker has no direct reason to make answers shorter. When every win shares a cause unrelated to your change, the win may not be real. It may come from how you measured.

The likely culprit is the **scorer**, the code or model that grades each answer. If it quietly prefers short answers, it rewards brevity rather than correctness. Shipping now could mean shipping a version that is only better at pleasing a biased grader.

"The scorer may be rewarding short answers" is better because it notices that the cause doesn't match the change, and it points you to check the measurement before trusting the result.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Nothing, causes do not matter once the count is…”?
check:0:2.a:
**What it gets right:** Counting the disagreements is how the lesson decides which version wins. That is the job of McNemar's test, from the Experiment design module.

**What it misses:** The count tells you *which* version scored better. It does not tell you *why*. The "why" comes from reading the traces. And here, the "why" looks wrong.

A reranker reorders retrieved documents. It is the step that decides which documents go to the top. It has no obvious reason to make answers shorter. So when every improvement shares the cause "answer is shorter", that cause has nothing to do with the change you made. The lesson says this is the moment to suspect the measurement itself. A **scorer** is the thing that marks each answer right or wrong. If the scorer favours short answers, the +3 may come from the scorer, not the reranker.

Ignoring the causes means you could ship a change that did not help.

**Why the other option is better:** "The scorer may be rewarding short answers" uses the causes as a warning sign and checks the measurement before trusting the +3.

check:1:0.q: Why not “The ones with the same result”?
check:1:0.a:
It's a natural pick, because those questions are the majority. With 200 questions, maybe 180 land the same way in both versions. It feels like the bulk of the evidence.

There is a small grain of truth in it. Same-result questions tell you the change didn't break those cases. A question both versions fail, like `charged-twice`, may also point to a weakness worth fixing later.

But they can't explain *this* change. If both versions got a question right, or both got it wrong, the change made no difference to the score there. Reading those traces is like studying two photos that look the same to find what moved. You'd spend most of your time on questions that say nothing about why the scores differ.

That's also why McNemar's test (the counting test from Experiment design) ignores them. Only the disagreements count toward the result.

"The ones where the versions differ" is better because those regressions and improvements are the only questions where the change actually altered the outcome, so their traces show what it did.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The claim that same-result questions 'didn't break those cases' is slightly loose for questions both versions fail, but it doesn't contradict the lesson.

check:1:1.q: Why not “A random handful from all 200”?
check:1:1.a:
A random handful does get one thing right. Reading real traces is how you learn what happened. Picking at random also stops you from choosing only the examples that support what you hoped to see.

The problem is where those random picks land. Most of the 200 questions got the same result from both versions. Both right, or both wrong. On those, the change made no visible difference to the outcome, so they can't show you what the change did.

Say only 8 of the 200 questions differ. A random 10 would include, on average, less than one of them. You could read every trace carefully and still find nothing that explains the change.

The questions where the versions disagree are called **discordant pairs**. They are regressions (old right, new wrong) and improvements (old wrong, new right). Every one of them is a case where the change flipped the result. That makes each one worth a side-by-side trace comparison.

"The ones where the versions differ" is the better answer because those are the only questions where the change actually changed something, so every trace you read can teach you something.

judge.notes: Minor: it slightly overclaims that the change caused every flip (the lesson says to suspect the measurement if causes are unrelated), and the point about random picks avoiding cherry-picking is not in the lesson. Neither contradicts it, and the answer is close to the 200-word limit.

check:2:1.q: Why not “The step that took the longest”?
check:2:1.a:
"The step that took the longest" sounds sensible, because slow steps often matter. But it answers a different question. Timing tells you about speed, which is called **latency**. A regression is about the *answer* going wrong. A step can be slow and still return exactly the same documents in both versions.

It does get one thing right: it makes you look inside the trace, step by step, instead of only at the final answer. That habit is good.

What it misses is the comparison. The slowest step might be slow in both the old and new traces. Then it tells you nothing about what changed. Also, once two traces split apart, every later step can look different too. Those later differences are often just knock-on effects, like dominoes falling.

So you scan both traces from the top. You look for the first step where they stop matching: different documents retrieved, a different order, a different tool, an extra loop.

**"The first step where they differ" is better because everything before it is identical, so that step is where the change actually took effect and caused the different result.**

check:2:2.q: Why not “The final answer's word count”?
check:2:2.a:
Word count is not useless. If the new answer is much shorter or longer, that is a real difference you can see. It can even hint at a measurement problem. The lesson warns about a scorer (the code that grades answers) that likes short answers. If every improvement is simply a shorter answer, word count would help you notice that.

But word count only looks at the very end of the trace. A trace is the step-by-step record of what the agent did. By the final answer, the real cause has already happened. Maybe the reranker pushed a policy document to the top. Maybe a different tool was called. Maybe there was an extra loop. A shorter answer is a symptom, not a reason. It tells you nothing about what to fix.

It is also too general to tally. "Answer got shorter" could come from many different causes. You could not group regressions into a clear pattern like "pushed worse doc up."

"The first step where they differ" is better because it points straight at the moment the two versions split, which is where the cause lives.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Find what changed, count the causes” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer**

*The problem.* "When I compare two versions on the same questions, one overall score hides what changed. Most questions get the same result both times, so they tell me nothing."

*The idea.* "I focus on the questions where the versions disagree. A regression is one the new version gets wrong but the old got right. An improvement is the reverse. For each one, I open both traces, the step-by-step records of a run. I find the first step that differs and label the cause in a few words. Then I count the causes in each direction. That shows what the change did and what to fix next."

*The edge case.* "If every improvement shares a cause unrelated to my change, I suspect the measurement. For example, the scorer might just like short answers."

**Likely follow-up**

"Why not just compare overall accuracy?"

*Hint:* Two versions can tie on accuracy yet disagree on many questions, with gains cancelling losses. Counting the disagreements decides whether the change is real. That is McNemar's test, which looks only at those questions. Reading them explains why.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **You only have one number.** The report says "score went from 70% to 72%" and nothing else. That small gain could hide 10 improvements and 8 regressions. The regressions are questions that now break, and nobody knows why.
- **The causes are vague.** Labels like "model did better" or "random" mean nobody opened the traces. A trace is the step-by-step record of one run. A good cause names a step: "retrieved the wrong doc", "called the wrong tool".
- **The causes don't touch your change.** You changed the reranker, but every improvement is "answer got shorter". That points to the scorer, not your change. A scorer that likes short answers can make a version look better when it isn't.
- **Surprises in real use.** Users hit failures on the same kinds of questions that regressed, because those were never read.

**Quickest check**

Pick two or three questions that flipped. Open the old and new traces side by side. Find the first step where they differ. If that step has nothing to do with what you changed, distrust the result.

Also check the arithmetic: improvements minus regressions should equal the change in the number of questions passed.

judge.notes: No clear problems. The answer matches the lesson, stays under 200 words, and gives no solution code. 'Reranker' and 'scorer' are used without a definition, which is a minor risk for beginners.

learn:stops.a:
**1. The answers are random from run to run.** LLMs can give a different answer to the same question even when nothing changed. Some "regressions" are then just noise, not caused by your change. Run each version several times on each question. Only count a question as a regression or improvement if it flips the same way every time.

**2. There are very few disagreements.** With only two or three discordant pairs, a pattern like "mostly moved the right doc up" is a guess, not a finding. Treat the labels as hints. Add more questions before you decide what to fix.

**3. There are too many to read, or the traces are long.** A big agent might take twenty steps per question. It might also disagree on hundreds of questions. Reading every pair by hand stops being practical. Read a random sample instead, say thirty pairs. Alternatively, let an LLM draft the cause labels and check a portion of them yourself.

learn:term.a:
"Disagree" is the bigger group. "Regression" is one kind inside it.

**Disagree** means the two versions got different results on the same question. One was right, the other was wrong. Statisticians call these **discordant pairs**, which just means "pairs that don't match."

A disagreement can go two ways:
- **Regression**: the old version was right and the new one is wrong. The change broke something.
- **Improvement**: the old version was wrong and the new one is right. The change fixed something.

So every regression is a disagreement, but not every disagreement is a regression.

An everyday comparison: you retake a quiz. The questions you answered differently are your disagreements. Some you got wrong this time after getting them right before. Those are regressions. Others you newly got right. Those are improvements.

In the lesson's example, three questions disagree:
- `return-label` and `refund-time` are improvements.
- `change-address` is a regression.
- `charged-twice` failed in both versions, so it's not a disagreement and gets skipped.

They work together like this. First you find the disagreements. Then the direction of each one tells you whether to call it a regression or an improvement. Then you label why it changed.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Four of those tickets needed no work to close”?
check:0:0.a:
That answer does notice something real: those 4 passes are strange, and something needs explaining.

But the question rules it out. Every task asks the agent to close an **open** ticket. So no ticket started out closed. And the do-nothing agent changes nothing. After its run, all 10 tickets are still open. None of them got "closed for free."

So the 4 passes can't come from the tickets. They come from the **checker**, the part that marks each run pass or fail. The do-nothing agent is a **no-op baseline**: a test agent that must score 0. If it passes even one run, the checker has a bug.

Blaming the tickets is risky. It shifts the fault onto the tasks, so you'd go "fixing" your eval data while the broken checker keeps passing false successes.

The likely cause is a judge that reads only the reply. It sees "Done!" and believes it. A code check like `ticket_closed`, which reads the real ticket status, would fail all 10 runs.

"The checker trusts the reply instead of the ticket" is better because it names the real fault: the checker grades the agent's claim, not the actual end state.

check:0:2.q: Why not “The real agent only has to beat 4 out of 10”?
check:0:2.a:
That answer treats 4 out of 10 as a fair starting bar, like a score to beat. It does get one thing right: comparing against a simple baseline (a plain reference agent) is a good habit.

But here the baseline should not score anything. Every task is "close an open ticket." The do-nothing agent closes nothing, so its true score is 0 out of 10. If it passes 4 runs, those 4 passes are wrong. That is not a bar for the agent. It is evidence of a bug in the checker.

And a broken checker breaks every score it gives. If it passed "Done!" on a still-open ticket, it can pass the real agent's false successes too. Those are runs where the agent claims it closed the ticket but didn't. So "beating 4" could still hide many failures. You can't trust the real agent's number until the checker is fixed.

"The checker trusts the reply instead of the ticket" is better because it names the actual fault: the checker reads what the agent says, not the ticket's real status. That points straight to the fix, a code check that reads the ticket table.

check:1:0.q: Why not “A judge with a friendlier rubric”?
check:1:0.a:
A **rubric** is the set of instructions a judge uses to decide pass or fail. A "friendlier" rubric is a more lenient one, so it lets more runs pass.

That is the opposite of what you need here. The judge already passed a run it should have failed. Being kinder means it would pass that run again, plus others it might have caught before. You would get fewer real catches, not more.

The deeper problem is what the judge looks at. It reads only the reply. The reply says "I've refunded the order", and that sounds like success. No wording in the rubric can reveal that the refund never happened, because that fact isn't in the reply at all. A stricter rubric wouldn't fully fix it either. A confident false claim still reads like a real one.

So this option gets nothing right for this problem. It changes how the judge grades, but not what the judge can see.

"A code check that reads the refund record" is the right answer. It checks the real end state in the system, so a false claim in the reply can't fool it.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Asking the agent to check itself”?
check:1:1.a:
Asking the agent to check itself sounds sensible. It does get one thing right: something should double-check the claim before you trust it.

The problem is *who* is checking. The agent is the one that just said "I've refunded the order" when it hadn't. Whatever went wrong the first time can easily go wrong again. Maybe it misread a tool result, or it assumed the step worked. So it will likely confirm its own claim.

It also has the same blind spot as your judge. It is still working from its own words and beliefs, not from the real world. A confident "yes, it's done" from the agent is just another reply. That is exactly what fooled the judge.

Think of a student marking their own exam. If they thought the wrong answer was right, they'll mark it right.

**A code check that reads the refund record is better because it looks at the actual end state, the real record in the system, so a false claim can't talk its way past it.**

check:2:0.q: Why not “6, the mistakes it caught”?
check:2:0.a:
The number 6 is real, and it matters. It's how many planted mistakes the checker caught. That count tells you about its **recall**: how many of the faults it found. Here it found 6 of the 10, so it missed 4.

But the question asks about **false alarms**. A false alarm is a good run, one with nothing planted, that the checker failed by mistake. The 6 caught runs aren't mistakes by the checker. They're exactly what it should flag.

Think of hiding 10 errors in an essay. The proofreader circles 6 of them. That's good work. They also circle 2 sentences that were fine. Those 2 are the false alarms.

So you look at two lists, two ways:
- Go through the planted runs and ask "was it flagged?" Yes is a catch (6), no is a miss (4).
- Go through the flagged runs and ask "was it planted?" No is a false alarm (2).

"2, the good runs it flagged" is right because false alarms count only good runs the checker wrongly failed, never the real mistakes it caught.

check:2:2.q: Why not “4, the mistakes it missed”?
check:2:2.a:
The number 4 is real. It just answers a different question.

You planted 10 mistakes and the checker flagged 6 of them. So 4 planted mistakes slipped through. Those are **misses**: bad runs the checker passed. Counting them matters, because misses are how a weak checker hides. Too many misses means low **recall** (the share of planted mistakes it caught, here 6 of 10).

But a **false alarm** is the opposite kind of error. It is a good run, with nothing planted, that the checker failed anyway. Misses come from the planted list. False alarms come from the flagged list.

Think of the two lists from the lesson:

- Walk through the planted runs: flagged means a catch, not flagged means a miss. That gives 6 caught and 4 missed.
- Walk through the flagged runs: not planted means a false alarm. That gives 2.

So "4" mixes up the two kinds of error.

"2, the good runs it flagged" is right because a false alarm means failing a run that had no planted mistake, and exactly 2 such runs were flagged.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Check the real end state, not the claim” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
An agent's reply is just words. It can say "I've closed the ticket" even when its tool call failed, or when it never made the call at all. Words cost nothing. The real result lives somewhere else: in the ticket table.

A judge that reads only the reply has no way to tell the difference. A confident "Done!" looks the same whether the work happened or not. So the judge passes it.

Here is what that looks like in real work. Say your support agent handles 200 tickets overnight. Its tool for closing tickets breaks after an update. Every reply still says "Closed it for you!" Your judge scores 100% pass. Your dashboard looks great. Meanwhile 200 customers are still waiting, and you only find out when complaints arrive.

A code check avoids this. It looks up the ticket and asks one plain question: is `status` equal to `"closed"`? That is what `ticket_closed` does in the lesson. It ignores what the agent claims and reads what actually changed.

The do-nothing agent is the quick test. It changes nothing and says "Done!". If your checker passes it, the checker is trusting words, not results.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Compare two lists both ways” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

**The problem.** A checker that misses mistakes looks just like one that works, because every run passes. So I plant mistakes on purpose and see what the checker flags. Flagged means marked as failing.

**The idea.** I compare two lists: the planted ids and the flagged ids. I check them both ways. First I walk through the planted list and ask, "Was this one flagged?" Yes is a catch. No is a miss. Then I walk through the flagged list and ask, "Was this one planted?" A no there is a false alarm, a good run failed by mistake.

**The trade-off.** You need both directions. A checker that flags every run catches every planted mistake, so it looks perfect if you only check one way. The second pass shows its false alarms.

**A likely follow-up**

*"What if no mistakes were planted at all?"*

Hint for a strong answer: "caught 0 of 0" means you cannot work out a catch rate (its recall). Report it as unknown, not as perfect. Then point out that this is why every test set should include planted faults, like the do-nothing agent.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs your checker is fooling you**

- **The pass rate is almost perfect, run after run.** Real agents slip up. A checker that never fails anything may simply not be looking.
- **Scores look great in testing, then drop in real use.** Users report tickets still open, while your results said "resolved".
- **Short, confident replies score as well as detailed ones.** If "Done!" passes as often as a real fix, the judge is grading the tone of the reply, not the result.
- **Your two checkers disagree.** In the results table, the judge's `resolved` column says pass, but `ticket_closed` says fail. That gap is usually a false success: the agent claimed it finished, but nothing changed.
- **Traces show no real work.** A trace is the step-by-step log of what the agent did. If it shows no tool call that updated the ticket, yet the run passed, something is wrong.

**The quickest check**

Run the do-nothing agent through your checker. It changes nothing and just says "Done!". It must score 0. If even one of its runs passes, your checker has a bug. Then plant a few false successes and confirm each one gets flagged.

learn:stops.a:
Planted mistakes work well, but here are three places they need extra care.

**Real mistakes don't look like yours.** Your checker can catch every fault you planted and still miss the kinds you never thought of. Also review a sample of real runs by hand, and turn each new failure you find into another planted case.

**Too few planted runs.** "Caught 1 of 3" tells you very little, because one lucky catch swings the number a lot. Plant several runs of each fault type, so recall (the share of planted mistakes caught) means something.

**The end state is hard to read.** A code-based grader needs a reliable place to check, like the ticket table. Sometimes the agent's action leaves no table to read, such as sending an email, or another process changes the ticket after the run. Run tests in a sandbox (a safe copy of your systems) and record the state right after each run. When there is no state to read, give the judge the trace (the log of every tool the agent called) instead of only the final reply.

judge.notes: No blocking problems; the third item runs to four sentences, slightly over the two-or-three guideline.

learn:term.a:
**They're the same thing.** In this lesson, "checker" and "grader" are two names for one job: marking each agent run as pass or fail. "Checker" is the plain-words name. "Grader" is what most people in the field call it. MLflow calls it a **scorer**, which is why the code uses `@scorer`.

Think of a teacher marking homework. You could call them the marker or the grader. Same person, same red pen.

The difference that matters is between **kinds** of checkers:

- An **LLM judge** reads the agent's reply and decides if it sounds right. In the code, that's `resolved`.
- A **code-based grader** checks the real result, such as reading the ticket table. That's `ticket_closed`.

In the lesson's example, the judge was fooled by `claim-1`. That run said "done", but the ticket was still open. The judge also passed the do-nothing agent, `idle-1`. The code grader caught both of those. Each one missed something on its own. Run them together, and fail a run if either one flags it. Then all 3 planted mistakes get caught.

check:0:0.q: Why not “The judge is good: 82 in 100 is high agreement”?
check:0:0.a:
The option gets one thing right. The judge really does agree with the humans 82 times in 100. That number is true. This raw share of matching answers is called the **observed agreement**.

What it misses is *why* they agree. Remember the lesson's example. If 9 in 10 answers are good, a judge that never reads anything and just says "pass" 9 times in 10 still matches the humans about 82 times in 100. Both sides say "pass" nearly all the time, so they line up by luck. A high count can come from a judge that is doing no real work.

That is the gap kappa fills. It takes away the agreement you would expect from luck alone and keeps only what is left. Here kappa is 0.05. That is very close to 0, and 0 means "no better than guessing." So almost all of those 82 matches are luck, not skill.

"The judge is barely better than guessing" is the better answer because it reads the kappa of 0.05, which strips out luck, instead of trusting the raw 82 in 100, which does not.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Kappa must be wrong when agreement is high”?
check:0:1.a:
It's a fair instinct. High agreement next to a tiny kappa looks like a contradiction, and a quick sanity check of your numbers never hurts. That's the part it gets right.

But here, kappa is doing exactly its job. It isn't broken.

Remember the lesson's example. If 9 in 10 answers are good, a judge that never reads anything and says "pass" 9 times in 10 at random still agrees with humans about 82 times in 100. Both sides say pass nearly all the time, so they line up by luck.

Kappa takes that luck away. Here, almost all of the 82 is luck, and only a sliver of real skill is left. So a kappa of 0.05 is the honest number. The 82 is the misleading one.

The option "Kappa must be wrong" trusts raw agreement over kappa. That gets it backwards. Kappa exists because raw agreement can fool you.

"The judge is barely better than guessing" is the better answer because a kappa of 0.05 sits just above 0, and 0 means no better than luck.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Judge B, a lower kappa is stricter”?
check:1:0.a:
"Judge B, a lower kappa is stricter" mixes up two different ideas.

Being strict means failing answers more often. Kappa doesn't measure that. It measures how much better than luck a judge agrees with the humans. A strict judge can have a high kappa or a low one. It depends on whether its fails land on the same answers the humans failed.

What the option gets right is small. A lower number does mean something real. But here the meaning is "closer to guessing," not "tougher."

Kappa works like this. Take the gap between chance agreement and perfect agreement. Kappa is the share of that gap the judge actually covers. Judge B, at 0.1, covers only a tenth of it. So its agreement with the humans is barely more than you would expect from luck alone. Judge A, at 0.75, covers three quarters of that gap. That is above the rough "good" line of 0.6.

"Judge A, it agrees well beyond luck" is better because kappa rewards agreement above chance, and A goes much further past chance than B does.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Neither, kappa can't compare them”?
check:1:2.a:
That option has a grain of truth. Kappa is one number, and the lesson says to use it alongside the pass-and-fail check, not instead of it. So you shouldn't trust a judge on kappa alone.

But "can't compare them" goes too far. Here both judges are scored against the **same human labels**. That means they face the same answers and the same mix of passes and fails, so the chance part of the sum is worked out on equal footing. Kappa also sits on a fixed scale: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than luck. Two kappas on that scale, from the same human labels, can be compared directly.

Read the numbers on that scale. Judge B at `0.1` is barely above guessing. Most of its agreement could come from luck, like the "always says pass" judge in the lesson. Judge A at `0.75` clears the rough "good" line of 0.6.

"Judge A, it agrees well beyond luck" is better because, with the same human labels, `0.75` shows real agreement left over after chance is taken away, while `0.1` shows almost none.

check:2:1.q: Why not “No, kappa replaces that check”?
check:2:1.a:
That option gets one thing right. Kappa is a better single number than plain agreement, because it takes away the agreement you would expect from luck. So a kappa of 0.7 does tell you the judge is doing real work.

What it misses is that kappa is still just one number. It blends passes and failures together. It doesn't tell you where the judge's mistakes are.

That matters because failures are usually rare, and they are often the answers you most need the judge to catch. A judge can earn a decent kappa while still letting a worrying share of real failures slip through as "pass." You only see that when you check passes and failures separately. That means asking how often the judge says "fail" when a human said "fail," and how often it says "pass" when a human said "pass."

So the two checks answer different questions. Kappa asks how much better than luck the judge is overall. The pass-and-fail check asks which kind of answer it gets wrong.

"Yes, use both checks together" is better because kappa shows the judge beats luck, while the pass-and-fail check shows whether it catches the failures you care about.

judge.notes: No real problems. The answer is about 200 words, right at the limit. The claim that failures are usually rare goes slightly beyond the lesson, but its 9-in-10-good example supports it.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Only if kappa drops below 0.6”?
check:2:2.a:
**What it gets right:** a kappa below 0.6 is a real warning sign. If kappa drops that low, you should dig in. So the instinct to check is sound.

**What it misses:** kappa is one number for the whole judge. It mixes passes and failures together. A kappa of 0.7 can look healthy while the judge still does badly on one side.

Failures are often the weak side, because they are rare. Say only 1 answer in 10 is a fail. The judge could catch most passes well and miss half the fails. The overall kappa might still look fine. But catching fails is usually the whole point of a judge. Those are the bad answers you want to stop.

Also, 0.6 is only a rough guide, not a hard line. Waiting for a single number to cross it means you might never look at the problem.

**Why "Yes, use both checks together" is better:** kappa tells you the judge beats luck overall, and the pass-and-fail check shows *where* it might still be failing, so you need both to trust it.

judge.notes: No clear problem. The claims that fails are rare and are the point of a judge go slightly beyond the lesson, but they don't contradict it and are framed as 'often' or 'usually'.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Count, then take away luck” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**The 30-second answer**

*The problem.* "Raw agreement can fool you. Say 9 in 10 answers are good. A judge that says 'pass' to nearly everything will still match the humans most of the time. It looks accurate, but it read nothing."

*The idea.* "So I count how often the judge and the humans really agree. Then I work out how often they'd agree by luck alone, based on how often each one says pass. Kappa is how much of the gap between luck and perfect the judge actually closes. 1 is perfect. 0 is no better than luck."

*The trade-off.* "Kappa can look harsh when fails are rare. A few misses on those rare cases drag it down a lot. So I report it next to the pass-and-fail check, not instead of it."

**A likely follow-up**

"What kappa would you need before you trust the judge?"

*Hint at a strong answer:* Give the rough guide: above 0.6 is good, above 0.8 is very good. Then say the bar depends on the stakes. A safety check needs a higher bar than a style check. Add that you'd log kappa with `mlflow.log_metric` and check it again whenever the judge's prompt or model changes.

judge.notes: No real problems. The rare-fails caveat, the stakes-dependent bar and the re-check advice go beyond the lesson but do not contradict it. The length is about 200 words, right at the limit.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Agreement looks great, but the judge rarely says fail.** If 95% agreement comes from a judge that says "pass" almost every time, it may just be riding along with your mostly-good answers. Kappa will be low even though agreement is high.
- **Bad answers slip through in real use.** The judge scored well in testing, then users find failures it never flagged. Often only agreement was measured, and luck hid the problem.
- **Kappa near 0, or below 0.** Near 0 means no better than guessing. Below 0 means worse than guessing. That often points to a bug, such as the two lists being in different orders, or pass and fail swapped.
- **Kappa missing or an error.** If every label on both sides is "pass", chance agreement is 1, and the formula divides by zero. You need some fails in your test set.

**Quickest check**

Put two numbers side by side in your MLflow run: plain agreement and `judge_kappa`. A big gap between them means luck is doing the work. Then count how many fails the judge gave, and compare that with how many fails the humans gave.

judge.notes: No blocking problem. Minor: the divide-by-zero point and the claim that a kappa near 0 'often' means a bug go beyond the lesson, though they don't contradict it.

learn:stops.a:
Cohen's kappa is useful, but there are a few cases where it needs extra care.

**1. Almost every answer passes.**
When nearly everything is "pass", chance agreement is already close to 1. Kappa then divides by a tiny number, so it can come out low or jumpy even when the judge looks fine. If both sides say "pass" every single time, kappa can't be worked out at all, because you would be dividing by zero. Lean on the pass-and-fail check from the previous lesson here. Also add more failing examples to your test set.

**2. Very few labelled answers.**
With ten or twenty pairs, one changed label can move kappa a lot. Treat a small-sample kappa as a rough hint, not a verdict. Gather more human labels before trusting it.

**3. Scores instead of pass or fail.**
Plain kappa treats every disagreement the same. On a 1 to 5 scale, a 4 versus a 5 counts as badly as a 1 versus a 5. Use **weighted kappa** instead, which gives partial credit for near misses. `cohen_kappa_score` supports this through its `weights` option.

learn:term.a:
**Cohen's kappa** is a score for how well a judge (here, the model grading answers) agrees with humans, after removing the agreement that would happen by pure luck.

**Everyday comparison:** picture a weather forecaster in a desert who says "sunny" every single day. They'd be right almost always. That sounds great, but they never looked at the sky. Kappa asks: how much of that rightness came from actually looking?

**The scale:** 1 means perfect agreement. 0 means no better than guessing. Below 0 means worse than guessing. As a rough guide, above 0.6 is good and above 0.8 is very good.

**In the lesson's example:** humans and the judge agree on 9 of 10 answers, so observed agreement is 0.90. But both say "pass" most of the time, so they'd agree about 0.74 of the time by chance alone. Kappa looks at the room left above chance (1 − 0.74 = 0.26). Then it asks how much of that room the judge really covered (0.90 − 0.74 = 0.16). That gives about 0.62.

So 90% agreement becomes "good, not great" once luck is taken out.

check:0:1.q: Why not “It stays at $18 a month”?
check:0:1.a:
"It stays at $18 a month" gets one thing right. $18 is the correct bill today, at 1 in 10. The price of a single score also stays the same, about $0.006, whatever you choose.

What it misses is that monitoring is not a flat fee. You pay for every score. The bill is the traces, times the **sampling rate** (the share of traces the scorer reads), times the cost of one score.

Scoring every trace moves the sampling rate from 1 in 10 to all of them. That turns 3,000 scores into 30,000. Ten times the scores means ten times the bill:

- 1 in 10: 30,000 × 0.1 × $0.006 = $18
- Every one: 30,000 × 1 × $0.006 = $180

That is why the lesson calls the sampling rate "the dial." Turning it up or down changes the cost in direct proportion. The usual advice is to score enough traces to catch problems, not every one.

"It goes from $18 to $180 a month" is better because it shows that scoring ten times as many traces makes the bill ten times bigger.

check:0:2.q: Why not “It goes from $18 to $36 a month”?
check:0:2.a:
The $36 answer gets two things right. It starts from the correct bill of $18 a month. And it knows that scoring more traces costs more. A trace is the record of one real conversation with the app.

What it misses is *how much* more. $36 is just double. That would only be true if you went from scoring 1 in 10 traces to 2 in 10.

The **sampling rate** is the share of traces the scorer reads. Scoring every trace moves it from 1 in 10 to 10 in 10. That is ten times as many scores:

- 1 in 10: 3,000 scores × $0.006 = $18
- Every one: 30,000 scores × $0.006 = $180

Each score still costs the same $0.006. So the bill grows exactly as fast as the number of scores. Ten times the scores means ten times the bill.

This is why the lesson calls the sampling rate "the dial." A small change in the share you score can make a big change in the monthly cost.

"It goes from $18 to $180 a month" is better because it multiplies by the true change in the sampling rate, which is tenfold, not double.

judge.notes: Only a minor looseness: calling the sampling-rate change "small" is odd when the example goes from 1 in 10 to every trace, and the answer is close to the word limit.

check:1:1.a:
"$60" is the price of one hour of an expert's time. It is not the price of the whole labelling job.

**What it gets right:** it uses the right rate. People cost money by the hour, and $60 is that hourly cost.

**What it misses:** it never counts how many hours the work takes. The question gives you the size of the job, and that is the step "$60" skips.

Here is the missing step:

1. 200 examples at 3 minutes each is 600 minutes.
2. 600 minutes is 10 hours.
3. 10 hours at $60 an hour is $600.

So the rule is hours times what an hour costs. "$60" uses only the second half of that rule.

This is easy to slip on because the rate is the only dollar figure in the question. It feels like the answer. But the question asks for the cost of the whole golden set. (The golden set is the batch of examples with the correct answers marked by hand.)

"$600" is better because it turns the work into hours first, then prices those hours.

check:1:2.a:
"$36,000" comes from multiplying all three numbers together: 200 examples × 3 minutes × $60. The first part is right. 200 examples at 3 minutes each is 600 minutes of work.

The slip is in the units. The $60 is a price per **hour**, but the 600 is a count of **minutes**. Multiplying them treats every minute as if it cost a full hour's pay. That makes the answer 60 times too big.

The fix is to turn minutes into hours first:

- 200 × 3 = 600 minutes
- 600 ÷ 60 = 10 hours
- 10 hours × $60 = $600

A quick sense check also helps. Ten hours of an expert's time is about one long working day. Paying $36,000 for one day of labelling should feel wrong straight away.

"$600" is better because it converts the minutes into hours before multiplying by the hourly rate, so the units match.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Score half of each answer”?
check:2:1.a:
"Score half of each answer" does get one thing right. The judge reads fewer tokens, so each score costs a bit less. (A **token** is a small chunk of text, roughly part of a word. You pay per token.)

But it breaks what the eval is for. The judge only sees part of the answer. A wrong fact, a missing step, or a rude closing line could sit in the half it never read. The judge would pass an answer it should fail. Now its verdicts are less trustworthy, and that is exactly what the question asks you to protect.

The savings are also smaller than they sound. The judge still reads the question, the instructions and any context. Only the answer part shrinks, so the bill drops by much less than half.

Compare that with sampling in production. Sampling skips whole traces, but every trace it does score gets read in full. Cutting each answer in half damages every single score.

"Batch the full runs, which can wait" is better because the judge sees the same examples and the same full answers, so the results are just as trustworthy, but batch processing (sending the jobs to run later in bulk) halves the price.

judge.notes: The answer is sound, but the claim that the judge still reads the question, instructions and context so savings are small goes beyond the lesson, and at about 200 words it is right at the length limit.

check:2:2.a:
**It does cut the bill.** Eval runs cost the examples times the price of one example, times every change you test. Fewer examples means a smaller runs line. So the option gets the cost part right.

**But it fails the other half of the question.** The question asks for a cut that keeps the eval just as trustworthy. Must-pass cases are the examples your app has to get right, no matter what. Think of them as the non-negotiables. If you drop them, nothing checks those answers any more. A change could break exactly what matters most, and the eval would still look fine. The bill shrinks, but you can trust the eval less. That is the trade the question asked you to avoid.

**Why batching is the better pick.** The full runs can wait for their results. So you can send them as a batch: a group of requests the provider handles later, at about half the price. You keep the same examples and the same judge.

Batching the full runs halves the cost of each run without removing a single check, so the eval stays exactly as trustworthy.

judge.notes: No real problems. The definition of 'must-pass cases' is not in the lesson, but it is a reasonable reading and does not contradict anything.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Price every line for a month, then find the big…” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**The 30-second answer**

*The problem.* Teams often budget evals by the judge's token price. The judge is the model that grades answers. But it's only one cost, so the real bill surprises them.

*The idea.* I split the bill into three lines and price each for a month. Runs: changes I test, times examples, times the cost of one example. People: hours spent labelling the golden set (hand-checked examples) and spot-checking the judge, times an hourly rate. Monitoring: real traces (records of live requests), times the share I score, times the cost of one score. Then I find the biggest line. Often it's people, not the model.

*The trade-off.* Monitoring has a dial called the sampling rate. Scoring 1 in 10 traces is cheap but can miss rare failures. Scoring every one costs ten times more.
